segments.say: Some time later, you find yourself walking again, slowly, on a path of packed earth beside a small stream. The night is soft and mild. The moon has risen, round and pale, and it lays a thin silver road across the water. And ahead, there's a very old stone bridge, with a single gentle arch.

show.title: A stone bridge over a stream

segments.say: Ines, the bridge inspector we've been picturing tonight, would have loved this one. The stones are fitted so carefully that no mortar shows. Each one leans on its neighbors, and they all lean together, so that the whole arch holds, and has held for centuries, through floods and frosts and many quiet footsteps. It's a lovely thing, to be held up by everything around you.

You walk up onto the bridge, and the stones are cool and smooth under your hand, worn round by all the people who have passed this way. Hundreds of years of travelers, with their baskets and their carts and their sleepy children, all crossing at their own pace, all arriving where they were going.

show.cap: An old stone bridge in the moonlight

segments.say: At the highest point of the arch, you stop, and lean gently on the low wall, and look down at the water. It slides past below you, dark and silky, with little points of moonlight dancing on it. It's making a soft, continuous sound, like a long, slow whisper. Hush, it says. Hush. Hush.

Listen to that sound. The stream has been saying the same thing for a very long time, and it never gets tired of it. The water that passes you now has come from the hills, and is on its way to the sea. It doesn't worry about the journey. It simply goes, and keeps going, the way water does.

There's something peaceful about that. The stream doesn't push, and it doesn't force. It finds the low places, and it fills them, and it moves on. Over time, it has shaped the whole valley. And all it has ever done is flow, one soft moment after another.
The water never hurries, and it always arrives.

show.text: The water doesn't hurry, and it arrives.

segments.say: If a thought comes into your mind now, you might imagine placing it on the water, like a small paper boat. You watch it float away, turning gently, getting smaller and smaller, until it's gone around the bend. And then another thought, if there is one. Another small boat, and it too drifts off, into the dark, into the quiet.
After a while, there are fewer boats. The surface of the stream is clear, and silver, and calm. The thoughts have found their way downstream, and the water is just water, and the night is just night.

And you stand there, on the old bridge, held by its stones, which are held by one another. Whatever else the night holds, you're held here. The stone is solid. The water is steady. The moon is slow. There's nothing to fall from, and nothing to climb to. You are exactly where you need to be.

You might feel a yawn coming now, a deep, slow one, and if so, let it come. Let your jaw open wide, and your chest expand, and then let everything sink back. A good yawn is the body's way of saying, thank you, I'm ready now. And the more you let it, the more it comes.

On the far side of the bridge, a grassy path leads gently uphill, toward a low stone wall, and beyond it, an orchard of old apple trees. They're in blossom, even though it's night, pale pink and white, glimmering in the moonlight like soft clouds that have come down to rest.

You can smell the blossom from here, a light, sweet smell, like fresh air and honey. It drifts down the path to meet you, and wraps around you like a soft scarf. You breathe it in, and each breath makes you feel a little lighter, a little sleepier, a little more at peace.

Before you leave the bridge, you look down at the stream once more. It's still flowing, soft and silver, and it will keep flowing all night, whether you watch or not. That's one of the quiet gifts of the world. It goes on, and it lets you rest.

And so you walk on, slowly, over the last of the stones, and onto the soft grass of the orchard path. Each step feels slower than the last. Each breath feels deeper. And the blossom trees open their arms to you, like old friends who've been waiting.
